readaloud.label: Cold Open — Arthur gets lost
readaloud.text:
Arthur Okafor has walked this route every morning for forty-one years. Left at the gate, past the postbox, right at the phone box, along the back of the park, home. He could do it in his sleep.

This morning he turns right at the phone box and finds himself standing in front of a house he doesn't recognise. He turns back. The postbox is gone. He walks for six minutes in a direction that should take him past the park, and arrives in a cul-de-sac he has never seen in four decades of living here.

His dog sits down and will not move.

Arthur is not frightened yet. He is seventy-two years old and he knows this street. He sits down on the kerb and waits. Someone will come. Someone always comes.

readaloud.label: Arriving at the Perimeter
readaloud.text:
Aldermoor looks like any other neighbourhood on a grey afternoon. Terraced houses, recycling bins out, a cat watching from a windowsill. The only signs anything is wrong are the small ones: a hand-lettered note on a front door that says DO NOT GO OUT ALONE. A ball of orange string tied to a garden gate, trailing away down the pavement and vanishing around a corner.

You can feel the boundary if you stand at it long enough. Not a wall. More like the moment before a word comes to you — that half-second of blankness where the thing you know perfectly well has temporarily left you. Except it doesn't pass.

readaloud.label: Entering the Zone
readaloud.text:
Inside the boundary, everything looks exactly the same. That's the problem.

The street is right. The houses are right. The corner with the post box is right — you passed it a minute ago. And yet when you look back, it isn't where it was. Not gone. Just slightly further than it should be. The distance between things is wrong in a way you can't quite measure, like looking at a room through a mirror and not immediately knowing why it's uncanny.

Somewhere nearby there's a chalk arrow on the pavement, pointing firmly in one direction. Someone drew it recently. Whoever it was knew something about this street that you don't yet.

readaloud.label: Climax — Feeling the Entity
readaloud.text:
You can't see it. You can't hear it. But here, at the epicentre, you can feel it the way you feel a very large room before you've counted everyone in it — a quality of attention that has nothing to do with sight or sound. Something vast and very old has noticed that you're here.

It isn't hostile. That's the strangest part. Whatever it's doing to this neighbourhood, whatever it's taken from the people who couldn't leave — it has no idea. It isn't cruel. It is just enormous, and it has been alone for a very long time, and it wants to be known the way it was once known, the way a place is known by the people who've lived in it for forty years. It just doesn't understand that it can't take that. It doesn't understand it's been taking anything at all.

handouts.label: Diane Marsh's Notebook — Selected Entries
handouts.body:
DAY 1
Got disoriented on Aldermoor Gardens — same street I've done three times a week for twenty years. Walked it twice and ended up back at the same corner. Not lost. The street is wrong, not me. Found the construction site office unlocked. Decided to stay put and observe. Rule one: don't make it worse.

DAY 2
The effect intensifies at dusk and again just before dawn. Clearest window is mid-morning, roughly 10am to noon. I've been timing it.

DAY 4
Animals are fine. I watched three cats cross the Gardens without hesitation. They know exactly where they're going. Whatever is disrupting the cognitive map, it doesn't work on them. Important.

DAY 6
Someone is leaving food parcels at the fence each night. I haven't seen who. I'm grateful.

DAY 7 — NOTE
Something in the excavation substrate. Dawn. Low light. There's a shape in the rock — not carved, not structural. The impression of a threshold. Like a doorway that was never built but is remembered anyway. I drew it. I don't know what it is. It isn't architectural.

[ SKETCH — one page — threshold shape, reservoir substrate ]

DAY 9
Someone will come. The effect has structure. It can be understood. I've been mapping the intensity cycles — I think the clearest approach is from the north, mid-morning. Whoever finds this: the string-line method works.

handouts.subject: EPICENTRE — STANDING DIRECTIVE
handouts.body:
Whatever you find at 14 Aldermoor Crescent — document it. All of it.

Don't destroy anything you can't replace. Don't attempt resolution before I've had a chance to assess what we're dealing with. We may only get one chance to study something like this.

I understand there are residents inside. I am not asking you to leave them there. I am asking you not to close a door we haven't finished looking through.

Those are not the same instruction. I trust you to know the difference.

— Leech

readaloud.label: Cold Open — Someone Had to Keep Things Going
readaloud.text:
The ward is quiet. A woman — mid-thirties, still in her coat, handbag over one arm — sits in the chair beside the bed. She has been here every day for eleven days. She is Daniel Ashworth's sister, and she has brought him a book he likes and some fruit he won't touch, and she is running out of things to say.

The man in the bed is sitting upright, hands folded, watching the window. He turns when she speaks his name.

"Danny." She says it gently. The way you say a name when you've stopped expecting it to work. "It's me. It's Sarah."

He looks at her with genuine warmth — really looks, the way actors learn to look, taking in an audience. Then he smiles.

"You brought the wrong book," he says. His voice is different. Not wrong — just older, settled, lived-in in a way that doesn't match his face. "Daniel doesn't like that one. He only keeps it because your mother gave it to him. He'd never tell you that."

She goes very still.

"He told me quite a lot, in the first few days," the man in the bed continues, pleasantly. "We've had a lot of time to talk. I'm Edmund, by the way. I know that doesn't help."

"Edmund Farrow died eight months ago," she says.

"Yes." He folds his hands again. "Daniel's fine. He's just — resting. I've been keeping things going. Someone had to."

readaloud.label: Scene 2 — The Rehearsal
readaloud.text:
The stage is set for Act II. Four understudies run through a scene from The Two Gentlemen of Verona — the same production, the same roles, the same choices Clara and Edmund made for three consecutive seasons.

It shouldn't be this good. The understudies are accomplished — that's not the surprise. The surprise is the specificity. The particular way the actor playing Proteus tilts his head before a line he doesn't trust yet. The way the actor playing Silvia turns upstage a beat before her cue, as if she knows what's coming from offstage before it arrives.

Petra Novak is next to you. She watches with the expression of someone witnessing something they cannot name and have decided not to try.

"That's the bit," she says quietly, not looking at you. "That's exactly the bit."

readaloud.label: Scene 3 — Rook at the Loading Bay
readaloud.text:
She's in the loading bay when you find her, tablet in hand, watching the building. She turns when she hears you, without surprise — she heard you coming from the stage door. She lets you get all the way to her before she speaks.

"PORTAL." She doesn't move. "Right on time." A beat. "I was wondering if you'd send the same team. I'm glad you did — I have questions."

She glances, briefly, at Sven. Something in her expression doesn't change, exactly, but it recalibrates.

readaloud.label: Climax — Fourteen Minutes to Curtain
readaloud.text:
The house is sold out. Fourteen minutes to curtain. Sophie Marsh is in the wings, script in hand, and she is more herself than she was yesterday — and also slightly less. The thing that has been slowly entering her is close to the surface tonight. She knows. She can feel it in the way she knows her next line before she reads it.

The stage manager calls places.

Backstage smells like greasepaint and timber and something older. The lights dim in the house. The audience quiets. And in the space between the last murmur and the first cue, there is a quality of attention in the building that has nothing to do with the four hundred people in the seats.

Clara and Edmund are ready. They have been waiting for this.

ENTRY — WEEK 6 OF CURRENT SEASON
Something strange in the Silvia scenes today. I knew my next line before I read it. Not memory — I've been off-book for weeks. This was different. It felt like remembering something that happened rather than something I learned.

ENTRY — WEEK 11
It's happening more. Making choices in rehearsal that I don't remember deciding. Edmund noticed — he said my instincts have never been better. He meant it as a compliment. I smiled and said thank you.

ENTRY — WEEK 14
I should tell Edmund. I keep not telling Edmund. I don't know how to say: I think something is happening to me that I don't have a name for, and it feels like excellence, which is the part that frightens me most.

ENTRY — WEEK 17 [final entry]
The touring production briefing is on Thursday. I've been planning this for two years. I want to see it through.

I want to see it through.

handouts.label: Scene 2 — The Rehearsal
handouts.text:
The stage is set for Act II. Four understudies run through a scene from The Two Gentlemen of Verona — the same production, the same roles, the same choices Clara and Edmund made for three consecutive seasons.

It shouldn't be this good. The understudies are accomplished — that's not the surprise. The surprise is the specificity. The particular way the actor playing Proteus tilts his head before a line he doesn't trust yet. The way the actor playing Silvia turns upstage a beat before her cue, as if she knows what's coming from offstage before it arrives.

Petra Novak is next to you. She watches with the expression of someone witnessing something they cannot name and have decided not to try.

"That's the bit," she says quietly, not looking at you. "That's exactly the bit."

handouts.subject: MID-DEPLOYMENT — STANDING DIRECTIVE
handouts.body:
Whatever you find in that theatre — document it.

The mechanism is significant. If the performance context is genuinely functioning as a BIM amplifier, that is something we need to understand before we close the case.

I am not asking you to leave anyone in danger. I am asking you not to destroy something we haven't finished studying.

Those are not the same instruction. I trust you to know the difference.

— Leech

handouts.label: Scene 3 — Rook at the Loading Bay
handouts.text:
She's in the loading bay when you find her, tablet in hand, watching the building. She turns when she hears you, without surprise — she heard you coming from the stage door. She lets you get all the way to her before she speaks.

"PORTAL." She doesn't move. "Right on time." A beat. "I was wondering if you'd send the same team. I'm glad you did — I have questions."

She glances, briefly, at Sven. Something in her expression doesn't change, exactly, but it recalibrates.

handouts.label: Climax — Fourteen Minutes to Curtain
handouts.text:
The house is sold out. Fourteen minutes to curtain. Sophie Marsh is in the wings, script in hand, and she is more herself than she was yesterday — and also slightly less. The thing that has been slowly entering her is close to the surface tonight. She knows. She can feel it in the way she knows her next line before she reads it.

The stage manager calls places.

Backstage smells like greasepaint and timber and something older. The lights dim in the house. The audience quiets. And in the space between the last murmur and the first cue, there is a quality of attention in the building that has nothing to do with the four hundred people in the seats.

Clara and Edmund are ready. They have been waiting for this.
